T01.name: Thoracic Facet (Zygapophyseal) / Mechanical Dysfunction

Localised paraspinal guarding.text: Reflexive splinting of the paraspinal muscles around the involved segment is a protective, nociception-driven response to facet/capsular irritation rather than a sign of structural instability. Its localized, single-level pattern (versus the global, multi-segmental guarding of an inflammatory or systemic process) points toward a mechanical facet source.

No neuro signs.text: A normal neurological screen rules out nerve root or cord involvement, supporting a facet/capsular source over thoracic disc herniation (T02) — the two share aggravating movements (extension, rotation) but this finding is the key differentiator.

Increased thoracic kyphosis.text: An exaggerated thoracic curve increases the flexion moment arm anteriorly and raises compressive/shear loading on the posterior facet joints and their capsules during extension and rotation — the movements that reproduce pain in this condition's functional screen.

T01.fma: Rotation & combined extension-rotation reproduce local pain

findings: Resisted trunk rotation/side-flexion — painless (non-contractile)
Passive rotation reproduces local pain with a capsular end-feel

cpa.pattern: Erector spinae compensating for the inhibited thoracic multifidus.

kineticChain.name: Thoracic Rotation Mobility
kineticChain.chainEffect: Rotation is the most thoracic-sensitive plane per Magee; restriction here forces lumbar over-rotation (disc injury risk) and cervical/shoulder overload above.

functionalScreen.name: Thoracic AROM Screen (rotation, extension, lateral flexion)
functionalScreen.note: Expect a local, reproducible restriction rather than the global pattern seen in T10.

T02.name: Thoracic Disc Herniation / Nerve Root Pain

Band-like sensory change.text: A band-like area of altered sensation tracing a thoracic dermatome reflects compression or irritation of a specific thoracic nerve root at its exit foramen — the hallmark sensory pattern of thoracic radiculopathy, distinct from the more diffuse or patchy referral seen in myofascial or facet-referred pain.
Band-like sensory change.source: Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment, Ch.8 (thoracic dermatomal pattern)

Possible cord signs.text: The thoracic spinal canal is narrow relative to the cord, and thoracic disc herniations are frequently central or paracentral, so a significant herniation can compress the cord itself rather than only a nerve root, producing myelopathic signs (e.g. lower-limb hyperreflexia, clonus, gait change). This finding should immediately escalate the case toward the T11 red-flag/cord-compression pathway rather than routine management.
Possible cord signs.source: Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment, Ch.8 (thoracic canal anatomy and myelopathy risk)

Guarded trunk posture.text: Protective splinting of the trunk musculature limits movements that would otherwise increase intradiscal pressure or foraminal narrowing and provoke the inflamed nerve root — a nonspecific but consistent finding across radicular presentations.

T02.fma: Trunk movement provokes dermatomal band; screen cord signs

findings: Resisted trunk flexion/rotation — rarely weak (mostly sensory)
Passive Slump/rotation reproduces the band-like dermatomal pain (neural, not contractile)

muscles.name: Diaphragm
muscles.state: Monitor breathing pattern if respiration aggravates pain (intercostal irritation)

cpa.pattern: Not a classic muscle-pair (MCC) compensation pattern — this is a neural condition; diaphragm involvement is monitored as an adjunct only.

kineticChain.reason: Not primarily a joint-mobility condition (nerve root); kinetic-chain testing is secondary to the neural findings above.

functionalScreen.name: T4 Syndrome Screen (+ neurological screen)
functionalScreen.note: Layered on a standard neurological screen when referred arm heaviness/tingling co-exists.

T03.name: Rib / Costovertebral-Costotransverse Dysfunction

Rib-angle tenderness.text: Point tenderness directly over the rib angle localizes irritation to the costovertebral or costotransverse joint at that level rather than the adjacent facet joint or disc, steering the differential toward a rib-specific rather than a vertebral source.

Altered breathing on one side.text: Asymmetric chest-wall excursion during respiration reflects a mechanically restricted costovertebral/costotransverse joint on the affected side, since normal rib elevation and rotation during inspiration depend on free motion at these joints — the same principle the Evjenth-Gloeck breath-hold test uses to localize a rib versus spine source.

Kyphotic / protracted posture.text: A kyphotic, protracted thoracic posture sustains the ribs in a relatively depressed, internally rotated position, increasing resting intercostal and costovertebral joint stiffness over time and predisposing to focal costovertebral/costotransverse dysfunction.

T03.fma: Deep breath & Evjenth-Gloeck breath-hold flexion localise rib source

findings: Resisted trunk rotation may reproduce pain if intercostals are contractile
Evjenth-Gloeck breath-hold test differentiates rib from spine source

cpa.pattern: Often co-exists with reduced lateral costal breathing on the affected side.

kineticChain.name: Rib Cage Mobility Assessment
kineticChain.chainEffect: The direct match: asymmetric expansion or a specific tender/hypomobile rib angle on PA spring test.

functionalScreen.name: Rib Mobility Screen (pump-handle upper ribs / bucket-handle lower ribs / rib spring)
functionalScreen.note: The same test as Rib Springing above, named as the app's functional screen entry.

T04.name: Thoracic Outlet Syndrome
recommended: Roos Test / Elevated Arm Stress Test (EAST)

Dropped shoulder.text: A chronically depressed shoulder girdle narrows the costoclavicular space — the interval between the clavicle and first rib through which the neurovascular bundle passes — a recognized structural contributor to compressive TOS.
Dropped shoulder.source: Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment, Ch.8 (thoracic outlet mechanics)

Prominent first rib on palpation.text: An elevated or prominent first rib narrows both the scalene triangle and the costoclavicular space, directly reducing the room available for the brachial plexus and subclavian vessels — the core structural mechanism proposed for neurogenic/vascular TOS. Note that TOS as a clinical entity remains diagnostically contested (no single reference-standard test), so this structural finding should be interpreted as supportive rather than definitive, consistent with this condition's low-confidence flag in the library.

Protracted / depressed shoulder posture.text: Protraction and depression of the scapula further narrows the costoclavicular interval and increases tension on the neurovascular bundle as it courses beneath the clavicle, reproducing or aggravating symptoms — the biomechanical rationale behind the Costoclavicular (Military Brace) Test.

T04.fma: Adson's / Roos / EAST reproduce arm symptoms; CRLF for first-rib restriction
T04.fascia: Scalene & pectoral fascial compression of neurovascular bundle

specialTests.name: Roos Test / Elevated Arm Stress Test (EAST)

findings: Resisted cervical side-flexion (scalenes) reproduces arm symptoms
CRLF (Cervical Rotation Lateral Flexion) is the passive Cyriax-style provocation test

kineticChain.name: Rib Cage Mobility Assessment
kineticChain.chainEffect: First-rib elevation and asymmetric expansion overlap directly with TOS mechanics; cross-check the Cervical Rotation Mobility chain too.

functionalScreen.name: T4 Syndrome Screen + cervical ULNT1/Adson's cross-reference

T05.name: Scheuermann's Disease
required: Observation (fixed vs correctable kyphosis on active extension)
recommended: Radiographic imaging (≥5° wedging ≥3 vertebrae, Schmorl's nodes)
posture: Fixed increased kyphosis not correcting on extension

Rigid structural kyphosis (adolescent).text: Reflects true structural wedging of at least three consecutive vertebral bodies (Sorensen criteria: more than 5° of anterior wedging per vertebra at the apex), producing a kyphosis that is fixed and does not reduce with passive correction — distinguishing it from the flexible, actively correctable kyphosis of postural round back (T06).
Rigid structural kyphosis (adolescent).source: Sorensen radiographic criteria for Scheuermann's disease

Apex tenderness.text: Tenderness at the apex of the curve corresponds to the site of maximal vertebral wedging and endplate irregularity, often with Schmorl's nodes where disc material has herniated through the weakened cartilaginous endplate during the growth-plate disease process.
Apex tenderness.source: Sorensen radiographic criteria; Scheuermann's disease clinical literature

Fixed increased kyphosis not correcting.text: Because the deformity arises from structural anterior vertebral body wedging rather than muscular imbalance, active or passive extension cannot reverse it. This fixed, non-correctable quality on extension testing is the key clinical differentiator from postural kyphosis (T06), where extension does reduce the curve.
Fixed increased kyphosis not correcting.source: Scheuermann's disease clinical literature (rigid deformity, uncorrectable by active extension or passive manipulation)

T05.fma: Prone extension does NOT reverse the kyphosis (vs postural)
T05.specialTestsNote: Only radiographic imaging is recommended for this condition (see Recommended above) — no manual special test named in the source.

findings: Resisted trunk extension weak relative to flexor tightness (lengthened over a fixed kyphosis)
Passive extension does NOT reduce the kyphosis (structural, not muscular)

cpa.reason: Not primarily a CPA pattern — structural/growth-plate diagnosis; imaging-led, not compensation-led.

kineticChain.name: Thoracic Extension Mobility
kineticChain.chainEffect: The fixed, non-correctable restriction over the foam roller is the key kinetic-chain finding distinguishing this from postural (T06) kyphosis.

functionalScreen.name: Thoracic Extension Mobility Screen (foam roller / chair test)

fields.label: Kyphosis at rest vs under extension load

functionalScreen.note: Document the fixed kyphosis at rest and under extension load.

T06.name: Postural Kyphosis (Round Back) / Upper Crossed Pattern
recommended: Thoracic MMT (lower trap, rhomboids, serratus anterior)

No structural change; fatigue-related ac.text: The absence of structural change together with pain that builds with sustained loading and eases with rest or postural correction reflects a motor-control and muscular-endurance problem rather than a fixed skeletal deformity — consistent with Janda's Upper Crossed Syndrome pattern of overactive/inhibited muscle pairs rather than the structural pathology seen in T05.

Slumped / protracted sustained posture.text: Per Janda's Upper Crossed Syndrome, tight pectoralis major/minor and upper trapezius pair with inhibited lower trapezius and serratus anterior, producing a sustained slumped, protracted thoracic posture. Because the driver is muscular imbalance rather than bony structure, active extension is able to reduce the kyphosis — the opposite of the fixed pattern in T05.

T06.fma: Symptoms build with sustained sitting, ease with postural correction
T06.specialTestsNote: No manual special test named — see Recommended above (postural assessment, Thoracic MMT).

findings: Resisted trunk extension weak but improves with cueing (motor control, not structural)
Passive extension DOES reduce the kyphosis (correctable)

kineticChain.name: Thoracic Extension Mobility
kineticChain.chainEffect: Expect a mildly restricted but correctable pattern (postural, not fixed); this drives forward-head posture.

functionalScreen.name: Thoracic Extension Mobility Screen + Scapular Stability Screen
functionalScreen.note: The upper-crossed pattern typically shows scapular dyskinesis alongside the kyphosis.

T07.name: Idiopathic Scoliosis
required: Observation (Adam's forward bend / skyline view, pelvic obliquity, shoulder asymmetry)

Rib hump on forward bend.text: Vertebral rotation accompanying the lateral curve carries the ribs on the convex side posteriorly, producing the visible rib hump on Adam's forward bend test. This combination of lateral curvature plus rotation (not pure lateral bending) is what defines a structural, as opposed to a purely postural/functional, scoliosis.
Rib hump on forward bend.source: Adam's forward bend test; adolescent idiopathic scoliosis screening literature

Shoulder/pelvic asymmetry.text: Asymmetric shoulder height and trunk shift reflect the compensatory curves and coronal imbalance that accompany a primary structural curve, and form part of the standard visual screening battery alongside the forward-bend test and scoliometer.
Shoulder/pelvic asymmetry.source: Scoliosis Research Society / USPSTF adolescent idiopathic scoliosis screening literature

Lateral spinal curvature.text: A measurable lateral deviation of the spine with associated vertebral rotation defines idiopathic scoliosis. An angle of trunk rotation of roughly 5–7° on the scoliometer is the commonly cited threshold for referral to radiographic Cobb-angle measurement, which matches the library's stated >5° referral cutoff.
Lateral spinal curvature.source: Scoliosis Research Society scoliometer screening threshold literature

Pelvic obliquity.text: Pelvic obliquity can act as either a compensatory response to, or a contributor to, the primary spinal curve, and should prompt assessment of leg-length and lower kinetic-chain factors alongside the spinal deformity itself.

T07.fma: Adam's forward bend / skyline view; scoliometer >5° = refer
T07.fascia: Asymmetric paraspinal fascial tension (concave vs convex)

findings: Resisted side-flexion may show asymmetric strength (concave shortened vs convex lengthened)
Primarily an observation + imaging diagnosis — limited STTT value

kineticChain.reason: Primarily an observation + imaging diagnosis, not kinetic-chain-driven; Thoracic Rotation Mobility may show side-to-side asymmetry as an adjunct finding only.

functionalScreen.name: Thoracic AROM Screen (L/R rotation comparison)
functionalScreen.note: Alongside the Adam's forward-bend/skyline observation above.

T08.name: Costochondritis / Tietze Syndrome
required: Observation (localized swelling — Tietze vs simple costochondritis)
observation: Anterior chest tenderness ± swelling at costochondral junction

Anterior chest tenderness ± swelling at.text: Reproducible tenderness at one or more costochondral junctions without swelling is typical of costochondritis (usually ribs 2–5, often multiple levels and bilateral), whereas a firm, localized, spindle-shaped swelling at a single junction — classically the 2nd or 3rd costal cartilage — distinguishes Tietze syndrome. The presence or absence of visible/palpable swelling is the key clinical differentiator between the two.
Anterior chest tenderness ± swelling at.source: Costochondritis / Tietze syndrome clinical differentiation literature (StatPearls; Physiopedia)

Protracted / slumped posture.text: A protracted, slumped thoracic posture increases resting tension through pectoralis minor and the anterior chest-wall fascia, which plausibly increases mechanical strain across the costochondral junctions. This postural link should be read as a plausible contributing factor, not a proven causal mechanism — costochondritis is generally idiopathic and this association is not well established in the literature.
Protracted / slumped posture.source: Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment, Ch.8 (anterior chest-wall loading); honest caveat on causal strength

Costochondral Junction Tenderness.text: Direct palpation reproducing pain at the costochondral or costosternal junction is the primary diagnostic finding for both costochondritis and Tietze syndrome, since there is no specific imaging or lab test for either — diagnosis is clinical and made partly by excluding cardiac and pulmonary causes.
Costochondral Junction Tenderness.source: Costochondritis / Tietze syndrome clinical diagnostic literature (StatPearls)

T08.fma: Anterior chest-wall loading (springing, arm horizontal adduction)
T08.specialTestsNote: No discrete named special test beyond palpation and resisted loading — see Palpation and STTT modules below.

findings: Resisted horizontal shoulder adduction / pec loading reproduces anterior chest pain (contractile/insertional pattern)
Passive rib springing reproduces local pain

cpa.pattern: Adjunct only; this is primarily a local insertional condition, not an MCC compensation pattern.

kineticChain.reason: Not a kinetic-chain-driven condition (local costochondral inflammation); Rib Cage Mobility testing would be positioned anteriorly, not the app's posterior rib-angle protocol.

functionalScreen.name: Rib Mobility Screen — anterior chest wall (pump-handle)
functionalScreen.note: Adapted to the anterior chest wall rather than the standard posterior rib-angle spring test.

T09.name: Thoracic Myofascial Pain
recommended: Thoracic MMT (lower trap, serratus anterior, rhomboids)

Taut bands.text: A palpable taut band is the defining physical sign of a myofascial trigger point — a localized region of sustained sarcomere contracture within the muscle — per Travell & Simons' integrated trigger point hypothesis, and is the structure from which referred pain is elicited on palpation.
Taut bands.source: Travell & Simons, Myofascial Pain and Dysfunction: The Trigger Point Manual

Trigger points (trapezius, rhomboids, le.text: Active trigger points in these three scapular muscles produce well-documented interscapular and periscapular referred pain patterns, and are classically driven by the same inhibited-lower-trapezius / overactive-upper-trapezius-rhomboid-levator imbalance seen in sustained protracted, slumped thoracic postures (cross-reference T06).
Trigger points (trapezius, rhomboids, le.source: Travell & Simons, Myofascial Pain and Dysfunction

Sustained-posture loading pattern.text: Prolonged static postural loading (e.g. desk work, forward-reaching tasks) is the classic perpetuating factor for myofascial trigger point development in the periscapular muscles, causing sustained low-level motor unit activity and localized muscle ischemia at the trigger point site.
Sustained-posture loading pattern.source: Travell & Simons, Myofascial Pain and Dysfunction

Trapezius.text: Trigger points in the middle and lower trapezius fibers refer pain along the medial scapular border, over the acromion, and into the posterior neck; taut fibers at these levels are frequently secondary to the sustained scapular protraction seen in slumped thoracic postures.
Trapezius.source: Travell & Simons, Myofascial Pain and Dysfunction

Rhomboids.text: Rhomboid trigger points lie along the medial scapular border and refer a superficial, localized ache in the interscapular region itself — one of the most common causes of a 'burning between the shoulder blades' complaint — and typically develop from eccentric postural overload as the muscle resists a protracted, kyphotic thoracic posture.
Rhomboids.source: Travell & Simons, Myofascial Pain and Dysfunction

Levator Scapulae (Table 8-8).text: Refers pain to the angle of the neck and along the vertebral border of the scapula — a classic 'stiff neck'/upper-back pain generator that is often mistaken for cervical facet or upper thoracic joint pain. Cited from Magee's Table 8-8 referred pain summary.
Levator Scapulae (Table 8-8).source: Travell & Simons, Myofascial Pain and Dysfunction; Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment, Ch.8, Table 8-8

Serratus Ant/Post.text: Serratus anterior trigger points refer pain along the lateral chest wall and can mimic cardiac or pleuritic pain; serratus posterior superior trigger points refer a deep ache under the scapula that can radiate down the posterior arm to the ulnar hand, occasionally mimicking a C8/T1 radicular pattern.
Serratus Ant/Post.source: Travell & Simons, Myofascial Pain and Dysfunction

Multifidus.text: Deep thoracic multifidus trigger points produce a localized, deep ache directly over the involved segment and can perpetuate the same segmental guarding seen in facet-related dysfunction (cross-reference T01), reflecting multifidus's role as a key segmental stabilizer that becomes locally hypertonic under sustained postural load.
Multifidus.source: Travell & Simons, Myofascial Pain and Dysfunction

Iliocostalis.text: Mid-thoracic iliocostalis trigger points refer pain upward toward the shoulder and laterally around the chest wall — on the left side this pattern can mimic angina — while lower-thoracic iliocostalis trigger points refer around toward the abdomen, a pattern that can mimic visceral pain. This wide, non-specific referral is why iliocostalis findings should always be interpreted alongside a red-flag screen (cross-reference T11).
Iliocostalis.source: Travell & Simons, Myofascial Pain and Dysfunction

T09.fascia: Myofascial trigger point / taut band network
T09.specialTestsNote: No discrete named special test — see Palpation and STTT/CPA modules below (trigger-point testing).

findings: Resisted tests reproduce referred (not true) pain from the palpated trigger point — no true weakness
Passive stretch of the muscle reproduces the referral

cpa.pattern: Classic driver of this referred myofascial pattern.

kineticChain.reason: Not primarily a joint-mobility condition (myofascial referral); Scapular Stability testing is the more relevant functional correlate below.

functionalScreen.name: Scapular Stability Screen (winging/dyskinesis)
functionalScreen.note: Scapulothoracic control quality is the relevant functional test since these are scapular muscles.

T10.name: Ankylosing Spondylitis / Inflammatory Spondyloarthropathy
required: Observation (FHP, flattened chest wall, flattened lumbar lordosis)

Global restriction.text: Uniform restriction across all planes of thoracic motion — rather than the local, single-segment restriction seen in T01 — reflects a systemic inflammatory process progressively ankylosing multiple costovertebral, costotransverse and facet joints simultaneously. This is the 'bilateral, symmetric, severely restricted' rotation pattern the library explicitly flags as a prompt to consider AS.
Global restriction.source: Modified New York criteria for Ankylosing Spondylitis; Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment, Ch.8

Morning stiffness posture.text: Prolonged morning stiffness that improves with activity (rather than with rest) is a hallmark inflammatory pain pattern, distinct from the mechanical pattern of T01–T03 which is typically aggravated by activity and eased by rest. It is one of the core clinical features supporting an inflammatory spondyloarthropathy over a mechanical diagnosis.
Morning stiffness posture.source: ASAS classification criteria for axial spondyloarthritis; Modified New York criteria

Flattened thoracic mobility.text: Progressive ankylosis of the costovertebral, costotransverse and facet joints flattens normal thoracic mobility over time, ultimately contributing to the fixed, 'bamboo spine' postural pattern seen on long-standing imaging.
Flattened thoracic mobility.source: Modified New York criteria for Ankylosing Spondylitis; AS radiographic literature

Reduced chest expansion.text: Chest expansion (measured at the 4th intercostal space) of less than 2.5cm relative to age/sex-adjusted norms is one of the four clinical criteria in the Modified New York criteria for AS, reflecting ankylosis of the costovertebral and costotransverse joints that restricts normal rib excursion during breathing — one of the few purely mechanical (non-imaging) diagnostic findings for the disease.
Reduced chest expansion.source: Modified New York criteria for Ankylosing Spondylitis

T10.fma: AROM uniformly restricted all planes; Forestier's bowstring sign

findings: Resisted tests generally painless early (inflammatory, not mechanical)
Passive ROM uniformly restricted, non-capsular pattern
Forestier's bowstring sign is the key positive test

cpa.reason: Not applicable — systemic inflammatory diagnosis, not a motor-control compensation pattern.

kineticChain.name: Thoracic Rotation Mobility
kineticChain.chainEffect: The library explicitly flags "severely restricted, bilateral, symmetric" rotation as a prompt to consider ankylosing spondylitis.

functionalScreen.name: Thoracic AROM + Rib Mobility Screen
functionalScreen.note: Reduced chest expansion on the rib screen is a hallmark AS finding alongside global AROM restriction.

T11.name: Serious Pathology / Red Flag
T11.body: Cardiac, respiratory, or cord-compression indicator → EMERGENCY same-day referral. Any other red flag (visceral, oncologic, infection, fracture) → URGENT referral.
T11.action: Replaces the differential list entirely when triggered. No module cards or test suggestions render. STTT/CPA: not applicable.
